title: What does “more standing” mean?
ask: You said a director or a lead has more standing than a junior developer. More of what?
eg: A lead wrote a decision and a junior then wrote over it. The junior's write replaced the lead's, with no conflict. There was no disagreement, so a rank would have nothing to decide.
run:
$ loops emit decision --of decision:kiln-schedule chosen=weekly      (the lead's key)
$ loops emit decision --of decision:kiln-schedule chosen=daily       (the junior's key)
$ loops of decision:kiln-schedule --plain
heads  1
  chosen  daily

options.choice: A rank. Where two people disagree, the higher one wins.
options.cost: The example is a replacement, not a disagreement, so a rank decides nothing in it. It would also have to say who may replace whom, and a junior's dissent is hidden.

options.choice: Counted or not, for the whole store.
options.cost: A junior's notes become proposals as well.

options.choice: Counted or not, kind by kind, with the right to accept what others propose. A junior's note counts; only a lead's decision does.
options.cost: A scope has to be written down. A set of kinds is the smallest one.

changes: What a grant holds, and so what IS4 writes.
from: From SL1. Nobody in the review broke it.

title: What does a read do with a record that doesn't count?
ask: A record may not count because its writer has no standing for its kind, or because its key doesn't speak for its observer. What does a fold do with it?
eg: The lead wrote monthly, then weekly. The junior wrote daily. The lead accepted it by writing daily, anchored on the junior's record. Read with the junior's record taken out, the lead's two writes come apart: taking the record out cut the chain between them.
run:
$ loops of decision:kiln-schedule --plain
heads  2
  chosen  conflict (2): daily | weekly

options.choice: Leave the record out before finding the heads.
options.cost: Accepting a proposal breaks, as in the example.

options.choice: Keep it in the order of what replaces what, and let it set nothing, its envelope included. Show it as proposed, counted beside the result. One reading for both reasons a record may not count.
options.cost: Every read gains a second part. An answer can change when a late grant or binding arrives, as it already does for a late prev.

options.choice: Include it and count it, as loops check does today with unbound.
options.cost: Nothing is canonical.

after: Under B the example reads chosen weekly with one proposal against it, then chosen daily once the lead accepts. That is proposed and not run: it needs the clause built. A record that can't yet be shown to count, because its grant, its binding or an envelope in between hasn't arrived, doesn't count yet. Admission keeps two answers.
changes: What a spec answers. The model, the vectors and Rust.
from: From SL2 and ID4, and item 1 of part five (margins).

title: How is a record tied to the store it counts in?
ask: And how is a grant tied to the grant that allowed it?
eg: One team lineage anchors a workshop store and a yard store. A grant written in the workshop is exported and imported into the yard, and the yard holds the same signed line with the same id. Nothing in it says which store it was for, and anybody can emit. The same goes for an ordinary record by someone granted in both.
run:
$ loops -C workshop emit grant --root --about sl:junior-example --about kind:decision
$ loops -C workshop export | loops -C yard import -
$ loops -C yard check
{"altered":[],"lines":1,"records":1,"refused":[],"segments":1,"unbound":0}

options.choice: Every record names one thing in under: its grant, or the store's anchor when it has none. Every grant names the grant above it, down to the anchor. Admission checks that the record's observer is the one its grant names and that its kind is one the grant covers, and the same of each grant above. A record under the anchor from anyone but a founder is a proposal to that store.
options.cost: Changes the bytes of every record written in such a store. A record counts by the one grant it names, so a second valid grant doesn't keep it counting when the first ends.

options.choice: A grant names its store among its mentions. Ordinary records name nothing, and admission searches for a grant.
options.cost: An ordinary record still replays from one store to another. A tree of grants over lineages can loop: the founder grants A, A grants B, B grants A.

options.choice: Nothing names a store.
options.cost: The example.

after: under is already an envelope field, “the record id of the grant it acts on”. Nothing writes it today, and nothing checks what it names beyond its being held.
changes: What a record holds, and what admission reads.
from: New in part five: items 2, 3, 17 and 20 (Neon, margins, Astra).

title: Where is a grant's scope written?
ask: A grant gives someone standing for some kinds of record. Where does it say which?
eg: Today a grant is an ordinary record. A spec that takes grants mentioning kind:note finds this one, and still finds it after loops erase.
run:
$ loops emit grant --root --about sl:junior-example --about kind:note --about kind:task
  about  kind:note, kind:task, sl:junior-example      payload {}

options.choice: In its mentions: exactly one grantee and the kinds. The store comes from under (IS3). The right to grant is a record kind of its own, carrying the kinds it may pass on.
options.cost: No scope finer than a set of kinds. Each kind becomes a thing, kind:<name>.

options.choice: In the payload, in spec vocabulary.
options.cost: A reader without the payload can't judge a record, so admission gains a third answer.

changes: What a grant holds. Permanent for every grant written.
from: From SW3, and items 7 and 20 of part five.

title: How does a grant end without taking past decisions out of the canon?
ask: When someone leaves, their grant has to end. Their past decisions have to keep counting.
eg: A director is granted decision in March and leaves in October. Their decisions from March to October must still read as canonical in November. A record signed with their key in November must not.

options.choice: An end is a record of the grant it ends, written by someone above that grant. It lists, as mentions, the topmost ids of a closed cut of what stands, and it ends the grants made beneath the ended one from then on. A record stands only if every end that counts covers it. Recommended before a team store is kept.
options.cost: A law of the model changes: holding more can now stop a writer counting, outside a cover. The envelope grows with the number of things the leaver wrote in. The verb refuses to sign unless its cut is closed.

options.choice: Nothing ends a grant yet. The host takes away the leaver's right to deliver.
options.cost: The host is the boundary for this case, and only for stores it carries.

from: From SW5, and items 2, 8, 18 and 21 of part five.

title: Does a cut follow under as well as prev?
ask: When a tick covers records you chose, does it also take in what those records stand on?
eg: A note under a grant under an anchor. A bare tick follows prev and under and covers three ids. A cut by ids or by time follows prev only, as documented, and covers one.
run:
$ loops tick spec.json                 covers 3 ids   {"answer":"same","closure":"yes"}
$ loops tick spec.json --cover <note>  covers 1 id    {"answer":"same","closure":"no"}

options.choice: A cut closes over under as well. IS5's end and IS8's continuing store are both explicit cuts.
options.cost: What such a tick covers changes. No record written today carries under, so no existing tick changes.

options.choice: A cut by ids or by time keeps following prev only.
options.cost: Not argued in the entry. An end (IS5) or a continuing store (IS8) would cover a record without what it stands on.

title: How is a second steward added, and who may end whom?
ask: A store starts with one steward. How is a second one added?
eg: The team's lineage founds the store and gives the lead the right to grant. The lead gives it to a second lead. The two fall out, and each tries to end the other.

options.choice: A second steward is a grant that carries the right to grant. A grant is ended by whoever is above it in the chain of under, and by nobody else. The founder holds no grant and is never ended. People are granted by the team's lineage directly, and a person's grant lets them grant its kinds to their own seats.
options.cost: Ending a lead's grant ends what that lead granted, which is why people are granted directly by the team.

options.choice: Stewards are equals who may end each other.
options.cost: The example has two consistent readings and no rule to choose between them.

after: Under A the second lead can't end the first, and the first can end the second. Left open: whether one of two founders may end a grant the other made.
changes: What admission reads of a grant.
from: From SW6, and items 2, 16 and 25 of part five.

title: What happens to records written before a store's anchor?
ask: Under IS3 every record ends at one store's anchor. What about records written before that anchor existed, or under an anchor that has to be replaced?
eg: A team's root key is stolen in June. The walk's first remedy was a new store that takes the old records as history. Under IS3, none of them would count in it.

options.choice: A store's anchor may name a tick and an earlier anchor. Records inside that tick's cover count as they did: records with no under from a store that was open, or records chained to the earlier anchor. For a root that was stolen, the cover stops before the theft.
options.cost: What a store's anchor holds, and what admission counts beneath it, change.

options.choice: A new store starts empty of standing.
options.cost: Not argued in the entry. The old records would not count in the new store.

changes: What a store's anchor holds, and what admission counts beneath it.
from: From items 19 and 24 of part five (margins, Neon).

title: What replaces promoting a record to a second store?
ask: The design had a record promoted from one store to another as the same record, so one erasure covers every copy. Under IS3 a record counts in one store only.
eg: A junior's proposal set chosen=daily and cleared day. The lead accepted it by restating the value alone, and the canon read chosen daily; day warm. Restating the clearing as well gave chosen daily; day —.

options.choice: Restate it: a new record with the same edit.
options.cost: A new id, so erasing the original doesn't reach it. A restatement by hand can lose part of the edit, as in the example, and two stacked proposals need their combined edit.

options.choice: Affirm it: someone with standing there writes an affirm stance, and the record counts there as it is, under its own id. Built with the first kept store. Restating stays as a verb for the trial, and it copies the edit exactly.
options.cost: A kind that admission reads before anything else.

options.choice: Ordinary records aren't bound to a store, so a verbatim copy counts wherever its writer is granted.
options.cost: IS3's example comes back for ordinary records.

changes: B adds a kind that admission reads.
from: From items 13, 15 and 24 of part five (Astra, Neon).

title: Who gets a lineage?
ask: What does an observer name: a person, a person in one part of their life, or a session?
eg: One person has a laptop from an employer and a machine at home, an agent harness on each, and writes in an employer's stores and in a public repository.

options.choice: One lineage for each person in each realm (work, own), and one for each harness of each person in each realm. A session or a worker is something a seat writes about, and gets none.
options.cost: Four lineages in the example. “The same person” across realms is a claim they may make and need not.

options.choice: One lineage for each person, everywhere.
options.cost: Every store that person writes in is linked by an id that no erasure removes.

options.choice: One for each session.
options.cost: No continuity for an agent.

changes: The observer in every record written afterwards.
from: From ID1. Not challenged in the review.

title: In the trial, is an observer a key or a lineage?
ask: The trial runs on stores declared disposable. Either way it has a store anchor and grants as records.
eg: One person in the trial writes from a laptop, a workbench and an agent.

options.choice: Keys, as today. Standing is built first, on what exists.
options.cost: The person in the example is three observers, with three grants. The plain views show keys.

options.choice: Lineages, declared disposable. One person is one observer from the first day, and the model of who speaks runs from the first day.
options.cost: IS2's reading for an unattributed record, and IS10, have to be ruled and built before the trial starts.

changes: Only the order of the work.
from: From items 10 and 22 of part five. Argued both ways in the review, and left to you.
